confidence_legend.official: stated by the manufacturer (Neural DSP, Shure, Royer, Celestion, York Audio...)
confidence_legend.community / widely repeated: multiple independent engineering or forum sources
confidence_legend.assumption: inferred or from general knowledge; not confirmed by a fetched source
confidence_legend.synthesis: derived here by combining sourced rules

meta.cab_field_notes: 'real', 'config', 'speaker' come from Neural DSP's 'based on' text. 'back' is not published by Neural DSP: back_confidence = stated (in the name), well-known (standard construction of that cab/combo), or assumption. 'character', 'pairs_with' and 'tags' are editorial summaries combining the speaker maker's description with general community knowledge; they are not Neural DSP statements.

mics_note: Neural DSP publishes no mic list and never names the real microphones (trademark-avoiding names). The current web manual (4.1.1) says only 'Cabinet simulation devices with selectable microphones'. Names below come from a screenshot in the official 1.0.2 manual and from user reports. Neural DSP staff (Aleksi) on the forum: 'Some of the cabs have a slightly different selection, but none of them have that many mics' - users see about 6-7 choices per cab. Code must read each cab's available mic list from the unit instead of assuming a global list. Real-mic mappings follow the naming convention shared with Line 6 Helix and Fractal DynaCab; none is confirmed by Neural DSP.

mics.character: Sub-200 Hz roll-off, slight suckout around 300-500 Hz, broad 2-12 kHz presence peak (SOS); peak 2-6 kHz (Recording Magazine); 'aggressive mid-range growl' (Premier Guitar). Tight, cutting, can be fizzy at cap centre.

Wider response than the 57 with no low-mid suckout and extra sensitivity above 1 kHz (SOS); on its own 'warm and full, with slightly rolled off highs' (Premier Guitar). Adds low-mid body and a different upper-mid edge.

mics.name_evidence: unverified on QC (appears in Neural DSP plugins and in a search-result summary of a GitHub issue that could not be opened)

'Big, ribbony sound' (Premier Guitar); slightly brighter than the R-121 (Recording Magazine). Smooth top with a tighter, more focused pickup than a figure-8 ribbon.

position.official_text: POSITION: Controls where the microphone is, from the center of the cone to the edge of the cone (automatically disabled when using external IR files).
position.effect_of_increasing: If 0 = centre (unverified): moving toward the cone edge - progressively darker, less fizz/bite, fuller low-mids; at the far edge the sound thins. Decreasing = toward the dust cap: brighter, more attack and fizz.

audible_effect_by_direction.toward_edge: darker, warmer, 'meatier'; extreme edge = thinner, reduced bass (Shure)

position.scale_note: Catalog range is 0..10 for factory cabs (0..1 for plugin cabs); the unit's screen shows 0.00-1.00 in manual screenshots (e.g. defaults 0.30 and 0.74).
position.confidence: official for the axis (centre-to-edge); assumption for which numeric end is the centre - no manual, forum post or measurement found states it. A feature request on the Neural forum complains the graphic is 'rather abstract' and asks for guides 'relative to the dust cap and speaker edge'.
position.how_to_verify: Render the same DI through one cab/mic at POSITION min and max, DISTANCE fixed; the setting with the higher spectral centroid / more 4-8 kHz energy is the cap centre.

distance.range_means: Mic distance from the speaker, 'between close to the cab and far towards the room' (manuals 1.0.2-2.3.0); 'distance of the microphone towards the speaker' (manual 3.0.0). No inches/cm are published.
distance.best_guess_low_end: closest to the grille (manual screenshots show both mics at DISTANCE 0.00 as the default)
distance.effect_of_increasing: If 0 = closest (unverified): less proximity bass, softer attack, less direct high end, more room/air; sounds less 'in your face' and eventually thinner. Decreasing = tighter, more direct, more bass from proximity effect.
distance.scale_note: Catalog range 0..10 for factory cabs; several plugin cabs expose only DISTANCE 0..1; John Mayer cabs expose ROOM controls instead.
distance.confidence: official for the axis (close-to-far); assumption for numeric direction and for any physical distance mapping
distance.how_to_verify: Render at DISTANCE min and max: the closer setting has more energy below ~200 Hz and a shorter/drier impulse; the far setting shows later arrival (delay) and more room decay.

rules.rule: Move the mic away from the cap centre toward the cone edge before touching EQ.
rules.why: SOS: 'miking the centre of the speaker produces the brightest sound'; moving toward the edge reduces highs and adds depth. A 12-inch driver beams its highest frequencies from the centre.

numbers.start: on-axis at centre, 1-2 cm from grille, then sweep toward edge

rules.rule: Treat mic position as the first tone control; EQ second.
rules.why: SOS: 'Using the mic position as a tone control invariably delivers a better result than relying on adding EQ after recording.' Nail The Mix: if you need to boost more than a few dB, 'the problem might be at the source (amp settings or mic choice)'.

rules.rule: For more cut/bite move toward the centre of the cone; for warmth move toward the edge.
rules.why: Recording Magazine: 'the closer you are to the center of the speaker cone, the brighter and more direct the sound will be'. Royer: off-centre toward the edge 'the sound will become progressively meatier and less bright'.

rules.rule: Do not go all the way to the cone edge for 'more body' - the outer edge thins out.
rules.why: Shure SM57 guide: 'On-axis with the edge of the speaker cone' = 'Thinner, reduced bass sound'. Neural DSP: moving toward the outer edge 'will decrease midrange'. The fullest spot is between cap edge and mid-cone.

rules.rule: Angle the mic off-axis to soften highs when the tone is too bright.
rules.why: SOS: 'rotate the mic to around 45 degrees off-axis'; 'The further you move it off-axis in this way, the more high end you'll lose.' QC stock cabs have no angle control, so use POSITION, a darker mic, or an 'OA' IR file instead.

rules.rule: Use distance to trade attack and bass against balance and air.
rules.why: Shure SM57 guide table for guitar amps.

rules.rule: For more body/thump move a directional mic closer; for less boom back it off.
rules.why: Shure: within 6 mm (1/4 in) a unidirectional mic 'boosts bass frequencies (by 6 to 10 dB at 100 Hz)'. SOS: backing a directional mic off lessens proximity effect. Neural DSP: closer 'captures a more direct and focused sound', increasing bass; farther reduces bass and adds room.

rules.rule: Place ribbons a little farther back and off the dome; they get bass-heavy up close.
rules.why: Royer: brightest R-121 sound is 'on the center of the speaker dome, anywhere from 2 to 6 inches from the grille cloth'; backing off develops 'increased tonal complexity and low end at distances over a foot'.

rules.rule: Choose mic type by the complaint: dynamic for cut, ribbon for warmth/less fizz, condenser for open detail.
rules.why: Neural DSP: ribbons give 'a warm and full-bodied sound with a smooth high-frequency response'; condensers 'a more transparent and pristine recording'; dynamics handle high SPL and the SM57 is 'a legendary choice'.

rules.rule: Blend Dynamic 57 with Ribbon 121: ribbon for body, 57 for bite; balance with the two LEVELs.
rules.why: Royer: the most popular rock approach is an R-121 with an SM57 or 421 - the R-121 provides body, the SM57 adds midrange and top-end bite. Premier Guitar: the R-121 is 'a perfect blend with an SM57'. More ribbon = warmer/less fizz; more 57 = more cut.

rules.rule: Blend Dynamic 57 with Dynamic 421 for a fuller, harder-edged rhythm tone.
rules.why: SOS: SM57 + MD421 is the most popular pair (Joe Barresi's main combination). The 57 has a 300-500 Hz suckout and sub-200 Hz roll-off; the 421 has a wider response with no low-mid suckout. Barresi: edge of the cone for a fuller sound, dead centre for brighter. OwnHammer's 'MDRN' mixes are 57 + 421.

rules.rule: Fredman: two 57s with capsules together, one on-axis at the cone centre, one angled beside it; blend to tame the on-axis fizz.
rules.why: Nail The Mix: on-axis mic within an inch of the grille gives punch and attack; the angled mic 'captures less of the super-direct ice pick highs' and adds body. Angle given as 55 degrees (traditionally cited as 45). Start with both faders equal. Not reproducible with QC POSITION/DISTANCE (no angle) - use IR files labelled OA/Fredman, e.g. York 57 + 57-OA or Mix 10 (57 + 57).

rules.rule: Pair a dark mic with a bright one rather than two similar mics.
rules.why: SOS (Steve Albini): pair a dark mic with a bright one, e.g. ribbon + condenser; Eddie Kramer: U67 + M160, or SM57 + MD421 + M160 tightly grouped.

rules.rule: Use the second mic's level as a fine tone control; small amounts matter.
rules.why: SOS (John Leckie): the second mic can sit 10-15 dB down and blends 20-30 dB down still change the tone noticeably.

rules.rule: Keep both mics at the same DISTANCE when blending; if the blend gets thin or hollow, flip one mic's phase switch.
rules.why: SOS (Bill Price): balance the mics and position one 'fractionally' so both are in phase at high frequencies; mics at five and six inches cause phase shift. Recording Magazine: if the combined sound gets smaller you have a phase problem. Cortex Presets: sum to mono and flip polarity if frequencies vanish - 'The Quad Cortex has a polarity flip on cab blocks for exactly this purpose.'

numbers.problem_example: one mic at 5 in, other at 6 in

rules.rule: Changing one mic's DISTANCE slightly while blending is a comb-filter EQ; use deliberately or avoid.
rules.why: SOS (Jack Douglas 'phase EQ'): add each mic while checking that it adds rather than cancels; flipping one mic creates filter-like effects. Shure's general rule for separated mics is 3:1 spacing.

rules.rule: When mixing third-party IRs, use minimum-phase (MPT) files, or align with the IR loader's DELAY and INVERT.
rules.why: York Audio manual: 'It is recommended to use the Minimum Phase files'; natural-phase files blended together give 'mellowed top end and varying degrees of shift in the midrange'; 'Minimum Phase files are preferred when blending with factory cabs.' Overdriven.fr: a 0.12-0.20 ms delay typically fixes alignment against non-MPT IRs; try blends of 75/25, 50/50, 25/75, 10/90.

rules.rule: With an external IR loaded, 'move the mic' by switching IR files - POSITION and DISTANCE are disabled.
rules.why: QC manual: both parameters are 'automatically disabled when using external IR files'.

rules.rule: Do not expect room tail or very fine low-frequency detail from user IRs on QC.
rules.why: QC manual: uploaded IR files 'will be resized to 1024 samples after being uploaded (21 milliseconds approx)'. York's files are 500 ms and get truncated on import.

rules.rule: High-pass rhythm guitars at 80-120 Hz in a mix; raise until the guitars lose weight, then back off.
rules.why: Nail The Mix: 80-120 Hz starting range, removing sub-bass that competes with kick and bass. Fractal forum consensus for cab low cut: 80-120 Hz, with 80 and 100 Hz the most common. Cortex Presets (QC metal): 'High-pass at 90 Hz'. York Audio (live): low cut around 70-80 Hz.

rules.rule: Low-pass high-gain guitars: start at 12 kHz and sweep down to about 8-9 kHz; with FRFR monitoring 6-8 kHz is common.
rules.why: Nail The Mix: start around 12 kHz, sometimes down to 8-9 kHz, to 'remove that nasty, ear-fatiguing fizz without making the guitar sound dull'. Fractal forum cab high cut cluster: 6-8 kHz (7.5 kHz often cited); yek: 5-7 kHz for FR monitoring. Cortex Presets: 'Low-pass at 8 to 10 kHz to tame any digital edge'.

rules.rule: With a well-mixed IR, avoid heavy high cuts for live use.
rules.why: York Audio's advice relayed on the Fractal forum: for live, 'Just don't use any high cuts or you'll get lost in the mix'; start with a low cut around 70-80 Hz; a single 57 gives a focused sound that cuts through, fuller multi-mic mixes suit studio-style tone.

rules.rule: Use wider filters solo/at home and tighter filters in a band mix; keep separate settings per context.
rules.why: Fractal forum: use HPF/LPF 'to help a tone sit in a mix, not to fix a bad tone'; one poster leaves cuts near minimum/maximum and trims later to fit the mix; another changes only the cab block's high and low cuts between practice and gig volume. Single-coil clean example: 80-140 Hz / 6-10 kHz. No source found gives separate published ranges for lead vs clean vs rhythm.

rules.rule: 'Fizz' = roughly 5-9 kHz (some place it lower, 3.5-4 kHz). Fix: mic toward edge, ribbon or more ribbon in the blend, lower LPF; notch narrowly rather than a broad treble cut.
rules.why: Nail The Mix chart: 5-9 kHz is 'the #1 enemy of DI guitars and amp sims' - 'Don't use a broad treble cut', find and notch the offending frequency. Cortex Presets: 'Slight cut around 4 kHz if the tone is fizzing'. Mic/cab fix is a synthesis of the position and mic-character rules.

rules.rule: 'Harsh / ice-pick' = 2.5-5 kHz, which is also pick attack. Fix: move off the cap centre, swap V30 for a Greenback/Creamback-type cab, or blend in a ribbon; cut surgically only.
rules.why: Nail The Mix: harshness 2.5-5 kHz - 'A surgical cut here can tame the ice pick sound without losing bite'; bite/pick attack lives at 1.5-4 kHz. V30 is the upper-mid-forward speaker (community: ~2-3 kHz spike); Greenback has 'restrained top-end' (Celestion).

rules.rule: 'Cab honk / nasal' = 800 Hz-1.5 kHz. Fix: choose a scooped speaker (G12T-75) or blend one in, or cut here; a boost here pushes the guitar forward.
rules.why: Nail The Mix: 800 Hz-1.5 kHz honk/nasal - cutting makes guitars 'less like a wah pedal'; the chart notes 'A careful boost here can bring a guitar forward'. Speaker choice is a synthesis from speaker characters.

rules.rule: 'Boxiness' = about 250-500 Hz (centred near 400 Hz). Fix: favour the 57 (it dips 300-500 Hz), reduce a 421/ribbon in the blend, pick a larger closed cab over a small open combo.
rules.why: Nail The Mix: mud/boxiness 250-500 Hz, 'cardboard box' at 400 Hz - 'Be careful not to cut too much, or you'll lose all the body'. SOS: SM57 has a slight suckout around 300-500 Hz; MD421 does not. Cab-size advice is a synthesis.

rules.rule: 'Mud' = 150-250 Hz; 'boom' = below ~150 Hz. Fix: increase mic distance (less proximity), raise HPF, prefer a 57 over ribbon/condenser, prefer a standard-size 4x12 or 2x12 over an oversized 4x12.
rules.why: Nail The Mix chart: 150-250 Hz is a 'major source of mud' - a slight wide cut cleans up. Shure: proximity adds 6-10 dB at 100 Hz up close; SM57 rolls off below 200 Hz (SOS). Royer: a close R-121 gives exaggerated low end. Cortex Presets: 'Slight cut around 250 Hz to clear up muddiness'. Cab-size advice is a synthesis.

rules.rule: For 'more body': move from cap centre toward mid-cone, bring the mic closer, add Dynamic 421 or a ribbon under the 57.
rules.why: Combines: edge = 'fuller' (Barresi, SOS), proximity bass (Shure), 421 has no low-mid suckout (SOS), R-121 'provides body' (Royer).

rules.rule: For 'more cut': move toward the cap centre, favour Dynamic 57 (or 414), reduce the ribbon, and consider a V30 cab.
rules.why: Centre = brightest (SOS, Recording Magazine); SM57 presence peak 2-12 kHz (SOS); C414 'cuts through a mix well' (Premier Guitar); V30 is the upper-mid-forward speaker (community description). Nail The Mix: a small boost at 1.5-4 kHz adds bite; Cortex Presets: 'Small boost around 2.5 to 3 kHz for note articulation'.

rules.rule: Dial presets at the volume they will be played; expect quiet-dialed presets to be boomy and piercing loud.
rules.why: Fractal Audio (quoted on its forum): players dial in modelers at low volume and unknowingly compensate for Fletcher-Munson, then at gigs 'the lows are boomy and the highs are piercing'. Line 6 forum: FRFR reproduces far more bass and treble than a guitar speaker, so it sounds 'thin and boomy' turned up. Note the direction: sources say low volume sounds thin/flat (inviting over-boost), not that cab sims are inherently harsher when quiet.

rules.rule: A cab sim is the close-mic'd recorded sound, not an amp in the room; tame it with cuts, darker mic choice or more distance rather than expecting FRFR to sound like a cab.
rules.why: Line 6 forum: in front of an amp 'centered on the cap the sound will be pretty harsh', off-axis it gets darker - a close mic hears the harsh spot; FRFR does not roll off highs and lows like a guitar speaker, so high and low cuts are needed. One Fractal poster narrows to ~180 Hz / ~4.5 kHz to mimic a real cab. No source found on headphone-specific voicing.

rules.rule: Choose a closed-back 4x12 for high gain, drop tunings and tight lows; an open-back 1x12/2x12 for cleans, edge-of-breakup and a softer, airier tone.
rules.why: Thomann: closed cabs - 'The basses are clear, tight, and defined', slightly more pronounced mids, 'a beam of sound to the front'; open cabs - 'somewhat warmer with a slightly reduced treble range', bass 'slightly softer'. 'For the most part, 4x12 cabs are designed with a closed back.' If a closed 4x12 'sounds a little too harsh', try 'a 2x12 cab with an open back'. The difference matters less when close-miked.

rules.rule: More speakers/bigger box = fuller; a 2x12 is punchier and more focused than a 4x12.
rules.why: Thomann: 'the more speakers there are, the fuller the sound'. York Audio on the Mesa 2x12: 'The 2x12 design brings more punch and focus than its 4X12 big brothers'.

rules.rule: Mix two cabs with complementary speakers (e.g. V30 + G12T-75) rather than EQ-ing one; pan slightly apart or blend in mono and check phase.
rules.why: Overdriven.fr: speakers complement each other - 'V30 + G12K100, V30 + G12T75'; combining IRs 'has the most important impact on shaping the global tone', finish with EQ; start by mixing two IRs. Cortex Presets: 'load two cab blocks in parallel, each with a different IR, panned slightly off-centre'. Fractal users blend a Mesa 2x12 57 with a 4x12 57 for live.

rules.rule: On QC stock cabs map requests to parameters: less fizz/warmer -> POSITION toward edge or swap/raise ribbon; more cut -> POSITION toward centre, more Dynamic 57; more body -> DISTANCE closer, add 421/ribbon; less boom -> DISTANCE farther, HPF up.
rules.why: Synthesis of the rules above applied to the QC cab block parameters (two mic slots with LEVEL, POSITION, DISTANCE, phase; HPF 20-500 Hz; LPF 500-20000 Hz). Numeric direction of POSITION/DISTANCE must be verified on the unit first.

rules.rule: Start with one Dynamic 57 near the cap edge, close, then add the second mic.
rules.why: SOS: start on-axis at the centre 1-2 cm from the grille and sweep toward the edge. A QC preset guide suggests 'An SM57 at 0 degrees on the cap edge is a reliable neutral starting point' and treats the cap edge as the most balanced position (seen in search results; the page blocked direct fetch).

york_mes_212_v30.description: York Audio MES 212 V30: 'based on a Mesa horizontal Rectifier 2x12 cabinet loaded with English made 70 watt Celestion Vintage 30 speakers. The 2x12 design brings more punch and focus than its 4X12 big brothers... The low end is deep and powerful, the midrange is balanced and complex, and the top end ranges from seamlessly smooth to biting aggression with tremendous note definition.' Ten mics, 79 single-mic shots ('multiple sweet spot, cap edge, and off-axis files') + 15 multi-mic Mixes = 94 IRs. 24-bit WAV at 96/48/44.1 kHz, 500 ms, Raw (natural phase) and MPT (minimum phase) versions.

qc_stock_equivalent.name: 212 CA Recto V30 98 (M)
qc_stock_equivalent.note: Same cab type (Mesa Rectifier 2x12, V30) - useful for A/B and for blending with minimum-phase York files.

york_mes_212_v30.naming: On the unit: 'YA MES 212 V30 <mic>-<n>' and 'YA MES 212 V30 Mix NN'. <n> = 1-5 are different sweet-spot captures: 'Numbers 1-5 DO NOT determine a capture's brightness, darkness, or speaker position. The numbers only determine which capture you're listening to.' 'OA 1-3' = off-axis shots (dynamic mics only), 'also taken from various parts of the speaker'. 'CE' = cap edge and 'CNT' = center: 'Certain mics include cap edge (CE) and center (CNT) captures for brighter options with more attack.' Mixes 'are given a number in order to visually simplify the file names'.

york_mes_212_v30.mixes_documented: The manual lists only which mics are in each Mix, not positions, ratios, intended use or tonal character. Mix 04 and Mix 09 are both listed as 'SM7 + 160'. York: 'If you like a particular mix, try exploring more combinations of those mics to fine tune your sound.'

move_the_mic_with_files.less fizz / warmer: go from CE/CNT or 57 to OA shots, to a ribbon (121, 160, 313), or to a Mix containing a ribbon (01, 02, 04, 09, 11, 12, 13, 14)
move_the_mic_with_files.more cut / attack: CE and CNT captures ('brighter options with more attack'), 57/421/906 singles, Mix 03 or Mix 10
move_the_mic_with_files.more body: SM7, 421, 121 singles or Mix 11 / Mix 12 (inferred from mic characters)
move_the_mic_with_files.basis: CE/CNT/OA meaning is from the York manual; the rest is inference from mic character and needs audition, since numbers 1-5 carry no brightness order

york_mes_212_v30.notes: York's documentation does not describe the individual mixes beyond their mic pairs and gives no rhythm/lead/clean starting points. Use minimum-phase files (York: 'It is recommended to use the Minimum Phase files'), especially when blending with QC factory cabs. QC truncates the 500 ms files to 1024 samples (~21 ms). POSITION/DISTANCE are disabled for external IRs. Use 48 kHz files on QC-class modelers per York's list ('48k - ... most modeling units').

cab_block.default_params: bypass<switch>, ir selector<string>, LEVEL[MIN_CABSIM_DB..MAX_CABSIM_DB dB], PAN[0..10], DISTANCE[0..10], POSITION[0..10], phi<switch>, GRID MODE<switch>, HPF[20..500 Hz], LPF[500..20000 Hz], OUTPUT VOLUME[-96..12 dB], IR NAME<string>
cab_block.structure: Two mic slots per cab block, each with a mic selector ('ir selector'), LEVEL, PAN (BALANCE in stereo), DISTANCE, POSITION and a phase switch; block-level HPF 20-500 Hz, LPF 500-20000 Hz, OUTPUT VOLUME. Each slot can instead load an external IR ('Load IR'), which disables POSITION and DISTANCE.
cab_block.stereo_ids: Stereo cabs are the same cabs; st_id is given per cab. The offset is +20000 for most ids but NOT for 12054/12055 (swapped) and 12078-12089 (shifted) - always map by name.

ir_loaders.params: MUTE<switch>, INVERT<switch>, IR PATH<string>, LEVEL[-96..12 dB], HI PASS[20..800 Hz], LOW PASS[1000..20000 Hz], PAN[-1..1], DELAY[0..25.0 ms], ROOM MIX[0..100 %], PRE DELAY[1..100 ms], REV HI PASS[20..800 Hz], REV LOW PASS[800..20000 Hz], SIZE<rotarySwitch>, GLOBAL OUTPUT[-96..12 dB], IR NAME<string>
ir_loaders.notes: IR Loader blocks add what the cab block lacks for third-party IRs: per-IR DELAY 0-25 ms (phase/time alignment between two IRs), INVERT, HI PASS 20-800 Hz, LOW PASS 1000-20000 Hz and a room reverb section. 'Dual' loads two IRs. Local IR storage is 1024 slots; uploaded IRs are resized to 1024 samples (~21 ms).
